title: Floating Offshore Structures
analyses: Local structural stress and buckling analysis
Extreme storm and survival condition analysis
Damage stability and compartment flooding analysis
Structural collapse and accidental damage analysis
scope: Applicable to semi-submersibles, FPSOs, floating production units, spar platforms, tension-leg platforms, floating wind platforms and other floating marine facilities.

models.text: The suite should implement Archimedes' principle, hydrostatic equilibrium, displacement and buoyancy relationships, metacentric stability theory, righting-arm calculations, hydrostatic restoring stiffness, free-surface correction, intact stability, damage stability, compartment flooding models and nonlinear hydrostatic equilibrium.

It should include Laplace's potential-flow equation, linear radiation and diffraction theory, Green's function boundary-element formulations, panel methods, wave excitation models, added-mass and radiation-damping calculations, Haskind relations, response amplitude operators, wave spectral response models, first-order and second-order wave loading, difference-frequency and sum-frequency quadratic transfer functions and nonlinear Froude–Krylov loading.

The suite should incorporate Newton–Euler six-degree-of-freedom equations of motion, Cummins' impulse response formulation, convolution-based radiation memory effects, nonlinear hydrostatic restoring, viscous damping, Morison drag, mooring restoring forces, riser reactions, ballast-induced mass variation and coupled nonlinear time integration.

Structural models should include classical beam theory, hull-girder bending theory, shear force and bending moment equilibrium, thin plate theory, shell theory, stiffened-panel buckling, ultimate strength analysis, nonlinear material plasticity, von Mises yielding, elastoplastic collapse, fatigue accumulation and fracture mechanics.

models.group: Slamming, green water and fluid impact
models.text: Applicable methods include Wagner water-entry theory, von Kármán impact approximations, nonlinear potential-flow models, Navier–Stokes CFD, volume-of-fluid free-surface simulation, sloshing models, shallow-water deck-flow approximations, pressure impulse methods and fluid–structure interaction.

These calculations should employ proportional–integral–derivative controllers, linear quadratic regulator methods, Kalman filters, extended Kalman filters, state observers, thruster allocation algorithms, constrained optimization, nonlinear model predictive control and disturbance estimation models.

The suite should support probabilistic compartment flooding, nonlinear flooding paths, hydrostatic stability degradation, collision-impact energy methods, nonlinear explicit dynamics, material fracture, progressive collapse and structural residual strength analysis.

The suite should combine potential-flow hydrodynamics with viscous CFD corrections, nonlinear time-domain floating-body dynamics with mooring–riser coupling, hull finite-element structural calculations with wave-load mapping, fluid impact CFD with structural deformation, and sensor-based state estimation with physics-based digital twins. Advanced stochastic modelling should support extreme response analysis, Monte Carlo simulation, response surfaces and reliability-based design.

Plate thicknesses, stiffener spacing, bulkhead geometry, structural frame dimensions, material properties and connection characteristics.
Mooring line geometry, stiffness, mass, pretension, line strength, anchor positions and soil properties.
Riser hang-off positions, riser stiffness, tension, dynamic reactions and connection characteristics.
Tank capacities, tank positions, liquid densities, ballast transfer rates and pump capacities.
Watertight boundaries, openings, permeability, flooding paths and damage-compartment scenarios.
Thruster locations, thrust capacities, thrust-direction limits, response times and vessel control parameters.
Sloshing conditions, slamming areas, green-water exposure and operational loading distributions.
Wave scatter diagrams, hull joint classifications, cyclic stress characteristics and required design life.
Loading and unloading states, storage levels, offloading conditions, production equipment loads and vessel operating configurations.
Collision energy, grounding conditions, hull breaches, mooring failure and extreme storm loading.
Minimum stability margins, motion limits, allowable accelerations, structural stress limits, station-keeping limits and compartment damage requirements.

subtitle: FPSOs, semi-submersibles, spars, TLPs, floating production units and floating renewable-energy platforms.
ic: The initial conditions shall define the floating structure geometry, hull displacement, draft, trim, heel, centre of gravity, mass distribution and mass moments of inertia. The initial ballast, cargo, process equipment and consumable loading conditions shall also be established.

Hydrostatic analysis shall begin from an assumed or converged floating equilibrium, with buoyancy balancing the relevant weight and external restoring effects. The initial position and orientation shall be consistent with the loading condition and hydrostatic stability characteristics.

For time-domain motion analysis, the vessel's six-degree-of-freedom displacements and velocities shall be initialized, together with its initial wave environment and mooring or tendon equilibrium. For fully coupled analyses, mooring tensions and riser reactions shall be consistent with the vessel's starting position.

Damage stability studies shall begin from a specified intact or already-damaged compartment condition, with initial flooding levels and watertight boundaries identified. Ballast-control analysis shall establish initial tank fill levels and available pump capacity.

Dynamic positioning simulations shall initialize the vessel heading, position, thruster states and control-system conditions. Fatigue and structural damage assessments shall include pre-existing cracks, corrosion losses and accumulated damage as applicable.
bc: The hull's wetted surface shall be subjected to hydrostatic pressure and wave-induced hydrodynamic loading. At the free water surface, the model shall apply the appropriate wave and atmospheric conditions for the selected hydrodynamic formulation.

Open-water boundaries shall accommodate incoming waves and outgoing wave disturbances without excessive artificial reflection. Current and wind boundaries shall provide the prescribed environmental forcing.

Mooring, tendon and riser interfaces shall transmit their coupled reactions to the floating structure. Structural boundaries shall represent actual hull continuity, internal bulkhead connections, deck loads and equipment supports.

For compartment flooding, openings shall permit water transfer according to pressure differences and opening characteristics, while watertight boundaries shall prevent flow unless damaged or intentionally opened.

Ballast analysis shall prescribe tank transfers, pump operating rates, valve states and permissible tank fill limits. Dynamic positioning shall apply controlled thruster forces and moments, subject to thrust limits and operating characteristics.

For slamming and green-water loading, the relevant hull or deck surfaces shall receive transient fluid impact pressures. Collision, grounding and accidental damage analyses shall include contact boundaries, impact velocity and the affected structural region.

calibration: Calibration should use offshore vessel motion records, towing-tank measurements, wave-basin experiments, hydrostatic tests, inclining experiments and hull structural monitoring.
Hull mass distribution, centre of gravity and hydrostatic properties should be calibrated or confirmed using weight surveys, tank soundings, inclining experiments and measured draft and trim.
Hydrodynamic damping, viscous resistance and added-mass characteristics should be calibrated against model-basin experiments, decay tests, forced oscillation tests and field motion measurements.
Wave excitation and response characteristics should be informed by measured response amplitude operators and vessel motion records across representative wave frequencies and headings.
Mooring and riser coupling parameters should be calibrated using measured line tensions, riser reactions, vessel offsets and dynamic response.
Ballast control models should use pump performance tests, tank volume measurements, valve response measurements and recorded ballast transfer operations.
Damage stability and flooding parameters should be informed by compartment flooding experiments, measured opening characteristics and available field evidence.
Slamming and green-water load parameters should be calibrated using impact-pressure measurements and controlled wave-basin experiments.
Dynamic positioning control parameters should be calibrated from thruster tests, vessel manoeuvring trials and operational station-keeping records.
Structural fatigue and deterioration parameters should be informed by hull stress monitoring, representative welded-detail testing and inspection history.
verification: Hydrostatic calculations should be verified using known floating-body geometries with independently established displacement, centre of buoyancy, waterplane properties and stability characteristics.
Hydrodynamic solvers should undergo mesh refinement, wave-frequency resolution studies, radiation and diffraction benchmark comparisons and consistency checks on fluid-force calculations.
Six-degree-of-freedom vessel motion models should be verified using analytical rigid-body benchmarks, prescribed force-response tests and independently calculated motion cases.
Frequency-domain calculations should be checked for correct phase, amplitude, damping and frequency interpretation.
Time-domain solvers should undergo time-step convergence, numerical stability and force-balance checks.
Coupled hull–mooring–riser calculations should be verified by comparing component-level solutions against integrated models under prescribed boundary conditions.
Damage stability and flooding calculations should be checked for hydrostatic consistency, water-volume conservation, compartment connectivity and correct treatment of free-surface effects.
Ballast calculations should be verified against prescribed tank transfers and vessel equilibrium cases.
Slamming and green-water simulations should undergo spatial and temporal convergence studies appropriate to the selected fluid model.
Dynamic positioning calculations should be verified through controlled thruster commands, environmental force cases and controller-response benchmarks.
Hull structural response and buckling calculations should undergo finite-element convergence and established structural benchmark testing.
validation: Floating structure hydrostatics and stability predictions should be compared against independent inclining experiments, draft surveys and physical-model measurements.
Vessel motions and response amplitude operators should be validated against towing-tank tests, offshore monitoring records or independent model-basin experiments.
Coupled mooring–hull–riser response should be compared with measured vessel offsets, motions, line tensions and riser reactions.
Slamming and green-water predictions should be evaluated using independent impact experiments with measured pressures, loads and observed flow behaviour.
Flooding and damage stability predictions should be assessed using compartment-flooding experiments and documented vessel damage cases where suitable data are available.
Ballast response should be checked against recorded tank levels, vessel draft changes, heel and trim.
Dynamic positioning predictions should be evaluated against vessel sea trials, recorded station-keeping accuracy and thruster utilization.
Global and local hull structural predictions should be compared with strain monitoring, structural load testing and independently documented damage observations.
Long-term fatigue and structural integrity predictions should be assessed against inspection measurements and documented hull deterioration.

geometry.text: FPSO hulls, semi-submersible platforms, spars, tension-leg platforms, floating production units, floating wind platforms, pontoons, columns, ballast tanks, compartments, internal bulkheads, structural frames and hull appendages.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for complete hull geometry, watertight solid models, deck arrangements, internal compartments, bulkheads, stiffeners, propulsion appendages and floating-platform assemblies.

geometry.cat: Specialized ship and marine hull geometry formats
geometry.text: NURBS-based hull surfaces, IGES hull-surface representations, DXF three-dimensional hull sections, structured hull offset tables in CSV or JSON, and documented XML descriptions of hull sections and compartment arrangements should be supported. Vessel hull models should also accommodate station-based offset data and reconstructed fair surfaces. Proprietary ship-design formats can be supported through dedicated adapters where their geometry specifications or export interfaces are available.

WAMIT-compatible GDF (.gdf), Hydrostar-compatible hydrodynamic mesh formats through suitable adapters, NEMOH-compatible mesh descriptions, triangulated hull surfaces and general panel meshes should be supported for potential-flow analysis where their format definitions are implemented. The importer should recognize wetted hull surfaces, panel connectivity, surface normals, coordinate systems, waterline boundaries and separate floating bodies.

Nastran BDF/NAS, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, CGNS, SU2, OpenFOAM polyMesh, VTK/VTU, MED, UNV and Exodus should be supported for applicable global hull finite-element analysis, local structural assessment, CFD, slamming and fluid–structure interaction.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, 3MF, LAS/LAZ, E57 and XYZ point clouds should be accepted for scanned hulls, existing vessels, hull damage reconstruction and nonparametric floating-body geometry. GeoTIFF and gridded bathymetric data should also be supported where seabed geometry is required for station-keeping or coupled analysis.
